Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding both atomic structure and quantum mechanics. He developed the Bohr model of the atom, which proposed that electrons travel in discrete orbits and jump between energy levels by emitting or absorbing light. As the founder and director of the Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen, he became the primary spokesman for the orthodox Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. He received the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics.

In 1913, Bohr developed his revolutionary atomic model, which modified Ernest Rutherford's planetary model by postulating that electrons orbit the nucleus in quantized, stable shells. Crucially, electrons emit radiation only when jumping between levels — not continuously as classical physics would predict. This model explained the discrete spectral lines we observe in hydrogen and other elements.

Bohr formulated the complementarity principle, which states that physical systems exhibit mutually exclusive wave-like and particle-like properties depending on how they are measured. You cannot measure both aspects simultaneously — the act of measurement determines which one you observe. He proposed the correspondence principle, asserting that the rules of quantum mechanics must match the predictions of classical physics when describing systems with very high quantum numbers, so quantum theory is a generalization, not a replacement.

With Werner Heisenberg, Bohr led the development of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, which advocates a probabilistic view of physical reality where a system lacks definite properties until it is observed. This brought him into famous debates with Albert Einstein at the Solvay Conferences. Einstein repeatedly challenged this framework with clever thought experiments, but Bohr successfully defended the probabilistic interpretation.

In 1936, Bohr formulated the liquid drop model of the atomic nucleus, treating it as a drop of incompressible fluid. This model provided the theoretical basis for explaining nuclear fission. He also proposed the compound nucleus hypothesis, describing nuclear reactions as occurring in two distinct stages: the capture of a projectile and the subsequent decay of the compound state.

During World War II, Bohr escaped German-occupied Denmark in 1943 by fishing boat to Sweden, and he eventually traveled to the United States to work on the Manhattan Project under the pseudonym Nicholas Baker. Werner Heisenberg was his most brilliant student and close collaborator; the uncertainty principle was developed under Bohr's guidance. Erwin Schrödinger's wave equation was incorporated into the Copenhagen interpretation. Max Planck's quantum constant was woven into Bohr's quantized model of hydrogen.
